sentences.text: 7 The present application/petition is Under Section 166 and 140 MV Act, 1988 and in order to succeed in the claim petition/application, it is for the claimants to prove that respondent no. 1's vehicle which allegedly caused the accident was being driven rashly and negligently by its driver/respondent no.1.

It was held in MAC APP NO. 334/13 titled as ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Ltd.Vs Jitender & Ors. that in order to claim compensation in a petition U/s 166 of MV ACT 1988, the proof of negligence is sine qua non to succeed in the claim petition.

entities.text: ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Ltd.Vs Jitender & Ors

sentences.text: In a petition U/s 166 MV Act, it is a duty of the claimants to prove that the accident was caused on account of rash and negligent driving of the driver of the offending vehicle.

It was also held by Hon'ble Delhi High Court in case titled as New India Assurance Company Ltd. vs.
Harsh Mishra and Ors. MAC. APP No. 592/2011 that Negligence is failure to take proper care which a reasonable man would have taken under the circumstances.

sentences.text: As further noted, the proof of negligence is essential before a person or his master can be held liable to pay the compensation as consequently held by Hon'ble Supreme Court.

As held in para no 17 of the that judgment "The question for consideration before me here is whether mere registration of a criminal case is enough to prove the negligence on the touchstone of preponderance of probabilities.
To my mind, the answer to this question will be in negative.
As stated earlier, negligence is failure to take proper care a reasonable man would have taken under the circumstances.

Though it is not always MACT No.

sentences.text: It is well settled that in proceedings arising out of a claim petition under Section 166 of MV Act based on fault liability principle, a person cannot be held liable unless he contravenes any of the duties imposed on him by the common law or by the statute.

In the case of a motor accident it is imperative that the claimants show by some evidence that the driver of the motor vehicle had been negligent in relation to the said vehicle and thereby had caused an accident resulting in bodily injuries or death or damage to the property so as to be held liable as the principal tortfeasor.
The owner's liability arises out of his failure to discharge a duty cast on him by the law, on the principle of vicarious liability.
Proof of negligence is necessary before the owner or the insurance company may be held liable for payment of compensation in a motor accident claim case brought under Section 166 MV Act.

sentences.text: Corporation (supra) we cannot understand it as having held that in all claims under the Act proof of negligence as the basis of a claim is jettisoned by the scheme of the Act.

In the context of Sections 166 and 163A of the Act of 1988, we are persuaded to think that the so called obiter observations in Minu B. Mehta's case (supra) govern a claim under Section 166 of the Act and they are inapplicable only when a claim is made under Section 163A of the Act.

Obviously, it is for the claimant to choose under which provision he should approach the Tribunal and if he chooses to approach the Tribunal under Section 166 of the Act, we cannot see why the principle stated in Minu B. Mehta's case should not apply to him.
We are, therefore, not in a position to accept the argument of learned counsel for the respondents that the observations in Minu B. Mehta's case deserve to be ignored.

In light of above, here, it is considered view of the Tribunal that nothing has been proved by PW2 Rajesh Kumar that he was actually present on the spot at the time of accident with his alleged truck which as per his testimony, he was allegedly getting repaired.

In the facts and circumstances, since the law declared by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Meena Variya is binding, there is no escape from the conclusion that it is the burden of the claimants in a petition under Section 166 of MV Act to prove negligence.

Should they find it difficult to prove evidence with regard to negligence, the option to have resort to no fault liability on the structured formula Under Section 163A of MV Act is always available to seek just compensation.
From the material on record and from the testimony of the witnesses, it is proved that the driver/respondent no. 1 is not responsible for alleged rash and negligent driving.
The petitioners failed to prove that the alleged accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the respondent no. 1.

In light of above, it is considered view of the Tribunal that the petitioners have failed to prove that deceasedRandhir Singh @ Randhir sustained fatal injuries in motor accident allegedly caused by rash and negligent driving of vehicle No. DL9SW 8423 driven by respondent no. 1Rohit Kumar.

opennyai_summary.ANALYSIS:
It was held in MAC APP NO. 334/13 titled as ICICI Lombard General Insurance Company Ltd.Vs Jitender & Ors. that in order to claim compensation in a petition U/s 166 of MV ACT 1988, the proof of negligence is sine qua non to succeed in the claim petition.
It was held by Hon'ble Delhi High Court in New India Assurance Company Limited V/s Devki &
Ors.,M.A.C. App. No. 165/13, decided on 29.02.2016 that:
5.
It is well settled that in proceedings arising out of a claim petition under Section 166 of MV Act based on fault liability principle, a person cannot be held liable unless he contravenes any of the duties imposed on him by the common law or by the statute.
In the case of a motor accident it is imperative that the claimants show by some evidence that the driver of the motor vehicle had been negligent in relation to the said vehicle and thereby had caused an accident resulting in bodily injuries or death or damage to the property so as to be held liable as the principal tortfeasor.
The owner's liability arises out of his failure to discharge a duty cast on him by the law, on the principle of vicarious liability.
Proof of negligence is necessary before the owner or the insurance company may be held liable for payment of compensation in a motor accident claim case brought under Section 166 MV Act.
It was held by Hon'ble Apex Court in in Oriental Insurance Company Ltd. v. Meena Variyal 2007 (5)
SCC 42 that: on a careful understanding of the decision in Gujarat State Road Transport Smt. Chand Kaur(Wife Of The Deceased) vs Sh. Rohit Kumar (Driver) on 21 February, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/167300186/
8
Corporation (supra) we cannot understand it as having held that in all claims under the Act proof of negligence as the basis of a claim is jettisoned by the scheme of the Act.
In the context of Sections 166 and 163A of the Act of 1988, we are persuaded to think that the so called obiter observations in Minu B. Mehta's case (supra) govern a claim under Section 166 of the Act and they are inapplicable only when a claim is made under Section 163A of the Act.
Obviously, it is for the claimant to choose under which provision he should approach the Tribunal and if he chooses to approach the Tribunal under Section 166 of the Act, we cannot see why the principle stated in Minu B. Mehta's case should not apply to him.
Had there any grievances regarding acceptance of Cancellation Report, the petitioners should have approached the Higher Authority regarding acceptance of Cancellation Report.
Furthermore, the alleged accident occurred on 04.03.2013 and Cancellation Report was filed before the Court on 02.09.2014 but nothing came out from the record that alleged eyewitness approached the Police Station or Court regarding his presence at the spot.
In light of above, here it is said that mere getting a person examined as an eyewitness mentioning that the person who has been examined is the person who actually witnessed the MACT No. 1542/16 Chand Kaur & Ors. Vs. Rohit Kumar & Ors.
accident cannot be relied upon until or unless it is proved by corroborated evidence.
Smt. Chand Kaur(Wife Of The Deceased) vs Sh. Rohit Kumar (Driver) on 21 February, 2023
In the facts and circumstances, since the law declared by the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Meena Variya is binding, there is no escape from the conclusion that it is the burden of the claimants in a petition under Section 166 of MV Act to prove negligence.
Should they find it difficult to prove evidence with regard to negligence, the option to have resort to no fault liability on the structured formula Under Section 163A of MV Act is always available to seek just compensation.
From the material on record and from the testimony of the witnesses, it is proved that the driver/respondent no. 1 is not responsible for alleged rash and negligent driving.
The petitioners failed to prove that the alleged accident occurred due to rash and negligent driving of the respondent no. 1.
